open-question.question: The documented Codex install route is `codex plugin marketplace add uHappyLogic/cairn-codex`, but that repository receives content only when a release publishes the `hosts/codex/` tree, and the live verification runs before any release. From which source does the live verification's plugin-install check add the marketplace and install the plugin?
open-question.applied-principle: Check tier claims against the live environment
open-question.recommendation: It installs the exact bytes a release later publishes as the distribution repository's root, through a source form the installed CLI's help lists, with no network, no GitHub write, and no change to the release flow; the snapshot's `file://` URL is not among the forms `codex plugin marketplace add --help` lists (a local path, owner/repo, an HTTPS or SSH Git URL), the pre-release publish hand-writes to a distribution repository outside a release, the root marketplace installs through an unproven nested path that users never see, and the post-release smoke check would put a Codex-only step into a release skill that names no host.
open-question.alternative: The plugin-install check adds the marketplace from a local path: the committed `hosts/codex/` directory in the cairn checkout, whose root holds `.agents/plugins/marketplace.json` and `plugins/cairn/`. It then runs `codex plugin add cairn@cairn`. The cairn repository gains no new file and nothing is pushed or published. The documented `uHappyLogic/cairn-codex` route is not run by the milestone, and no later check of it is added. It installs the exact bytes that a release later publishes verbatim as the distribution repository's root. That covers the marketplace file, the `./plugins/cairn` source path and the `.codex-plugin/plugin.json` manifest, so it tests the recorded install layout. It needs no network, no GitHub write and no change to the release flow, and it uses a source form `codex plugin marketplace add` documents (a local path). It never runs Codex's `owner/repo` fetch path, which is how users really install. If the GitHub source is cloned or resolved differently from a local path, that difference first shows up for users after the release. The install is also user-level and points at the checkout's working tree, so the entry stays in the maintainer's Codex config after the throwaway workspace is deleted, unless it is removed by hand.

The check adds the marketplace from a Git source rather than a plain directory. A throwaway git repository is built in a temporary directory whose root commit is the `hosts/codex/` tree, the same tree-to-commit step the release skill uses to publish (`git commit-tree` of that subtree). That repository is added through a `file://` Git URL, then `codex plugin add cairn@cairn` runs. Nothing is pushed or published, and the cairn repository gains no file. The documented GitHub route is not run by the milestone. It runs Codex's Git-source install path against a repository shaped exactly like the future `uHappyLogic/cairn-codex`: the tree is at the repository root as a commit, not a directory inside a checkout. This gets as close to the documented route as possible without writing to GitHub. It adds snapshot-building steps to a verification that the recorded Verification workspace decision keeps unscripted and deletes afterwards. It still skips the GitHub `owner/repo` shorthand and network fetch, so the documented command itself stays unproven until users run it.

Before the live verification, the `hosts/codex/` tree is published into `uHappyLogic/cairn-codex` on a dedicated non-default ref (or a throwaway branch), using the same tree-to-commit step the release uses. The check then runs the documented command with that ref, `codex plugin marketplace add uHappyLogic/cairn-codex@<ref>`, followed by `codex plugin add cairn@cairn`. After the run the ref is deleted, so the first release can still publish the repository's root commit. It is the only option that runs the documented install command, through GitHub's `owner/repo` source, before release. Every part of the user's install path is then backed by the live run. It writes to a distribution repository outside `/release-plugin`, which goes against the rule that those repositories receive content only through a release and are never hand-edited. It also needs the clean-up step, or the release's expectation that the first publish becomes the root commit breaks. It only works if `uHappyLogic/cairn-codex` exists during the milestone, which is the axis the Distribution repository creation question owns.

The cairn repository gains a root `.agents/plugins/marketplace.json`, the Codex counterpart of the existing root `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json`. Its one `cairn` entry has a `source` path of `./hosts/codex/plugins/cairn`. The check adds the marketplace from the cairn checkout's local path, or from `uHappyLogic/cairn@<branch>` once the branch is pushed (the main repository is public), then runs `codex plugin add cairn@cairn`. The published tree's own marketplace file is not the one installed from, and the documented route is not run by the milestone. It gives the maintainer a lasting development install route for Codex that matches the one Claude Code already has. In its GitHub form it also runs Codex's `owner/repo` fetch path against a public repository, with no write to any distribution repository. It installs through a marketplace file that users never see, with a nested cross-directory source path that no shipped Codex marketplace has been seen to use. That is the kind of unproven path the Codex install route decision avoided. Meanwhile the `hosts/codex/.agents/plugins/marketplace.json` that users do get goes unchecked. It also adds a root file the build does not validate today.

alternative.id: Local tree plus release smoke check

open-question.alternative: The milestone's plugin-install check adds the marketplace from the committed local `hosts/codex/` directory and runs `codex plugin add cairn@cairn`, the same source as Local committed tree. In addition, the documented route `codex plugin marketplace add uHappyLogic/cairn-codex` followed by `codex plugin add cairn@cairn` is checked once, right after the first Codex release publishes the repository. That post-release step is recorded for the maintainer, for example as a closing step of the release skill, and calls no model. The pre-release verification keeps the local route's exact-bytes, no-publication guarantees. The documented command still gets run against the real repository at the first moment it can work, so a GitHub-source difference is caught by the maintainer rather than reported by users. The documented route is still unproven when the milestone is declared release-ready, and any failure it finds surfaces after publication, when fixing it costs a follow-up release. It also adds a post-release step to the release flow or the maintainer's checklist, which the milestone's four-check verification does not otherwise need.

open-question.question: The goal lists the `uHappyLogic/cairn-codex` distribution repository as part of the release-ready surface, while the release skill's pre-flight already stops on a missing repository and prints the `gh repo create` and `gh repo edit` commands, and the traffic-token step is deferred to the first Codex release. open-question.alternative: The repository is not created in this milestone and the task list has no task for it. At the first Codex release, the release skill's existing step-2f pre-flight finds `uHappyLogic/cairn-codex` missing, stops, and prints the `gh repo create` and `gh repo edit` commands. The maintainer runs them then. At that same release, the maintainer also extends the `TRAFFIC_TOKEN` as the recorded Traffic token extension decision describes. The goal's mention of the repository is met by the release path already handling it, not by the repository existing. It adds no work and no new mechanism, because the host-agnostic pre-flight already covers a missing repository by design. It also puts all one-time provisioning for the new host at one moment, the first Codex release. That is where the token step already sits, and the token cannot be extended to a repository that does not yet exist. The goal names the `uHappyLogic/cairn-codex` repository among the release-ready surface, so this reading leaves that item unbuilt when the milestone ends. It holds only if "release-ready" means the release path is ready. Otherwise the goal needs an edit through `modify-milestone-goal`. Until the release, the install route documented on `main` names a repository that does not exist. The first Codex release also stops at least once at pre-flight and has to be re-run after the maintainer acts.

The empty `uHappyLogic/cairn-codex` repository is created during this milestone by the maintainer, by hand. The maintainer runs the same two commands the release skill's step 2f prints: a public `gh repo create` with the fixed description and no license, README or gitignore, then `gh repo edit` to add the `cairn`, `codex` and `plugin` topics and disable issues, wiki and projects. The milestone's task list holds a task that stops until the repository exists and then records a read-only `gh repo view` read-back of its existence and settings in `TASKS_DONE.md`. No content is pushed and the `TRAFFIC_TOKEN` secret is not set, so the first publish is still the root commit at the first Codex release. It meets the goal's wording literally, because the distribution repository it lists as part of the release-ready surface exists when the milestone ends. It also follows milestone 23, where the maintainer created both existing distribution repositories inside the milestone that introduced them, and it reserves the `cairn-codex` name now. It does not save the first Codex release a stop. The recorded Traffic token extension decision defers the token step to that release and adds a pre-flight stop on the missing secret, so that run stops anyway. Until that release, a public, empty repository is visible with nothing in it. The manual step also breaks a headless run of the task list, because the runner has to wait for the maintainer.

The empty `uHappyLogic/cairn-codex` repository is created during this milestone by the task runner, not by hand. A task in the milestone runs the release skill's two step-2f commands with the already-authenticated `gh`: a public, deliberately empty `gh repo create` with the fixed description, then `gh repo edit` for the topics and to disable issues, wiki and projects. The same task reads the result back with `gh repo view` and records it in `TASKS_DONE.md`. No content is pushed and the `TRAFFIC_TOKEN` secret is not set. It is the only way to have the repository exist at milestone end with no handoff to the maintainer. The task list stays fully automatable and headless, and the read-back of the settings becomes part of the recorded evidence. An agent would perform a public act that cannot be undone, and both milestone 23 and the release skill reserve that act to the maintainer. The release skill says of these same commands that the skill must never run them. As with the maintainer option, the first Codex release still stops on the missing `TRAFFIC_TOKEN` secret, and an empty public repository sits visible until then.

open-question.question: The Codex README template opens with that repository's two traffic badges and the root README's adoption table would gain a `cairn-codex` row, but the badge images are served from a `traffic-data` branch that cannot exist until the repository is published, the `TRAFFIC_TOKEN` is extended, and the workflow has run once, all of which happen at or after the first Codex release. recommendation.option: Strip now, row after seed (release-skill prompt)

open-question.recommendation: The landing page never shows a broken badge, in line with the seed-before-reference order the existing badges followed, while the template keeps the shape the other two hosts share and needs no second release; the follow-up rides in the host-neutral instructions the release skill prints for a missing traffic token, so it reaches the maintainer at the one release where it becomes possible instead of resting on a note in a finished milestone.

alternative.id: Strip now, row after seed (release-skill prompt)

open-question.alternative: The Codex README template carries its badge strip from the start, so the first Codex release publishes it. The root adoption-table row is added only after the seed run. That follow-up is carried by the release skill: the host-neutral instructions it already prints when a distribution repository lacks the `TRAFFIC_TOKEN` secret gain steps that name no host. After publishing, run the repository's `traffic-badges` workflow once by `workflow_dispatch`, then add the repository's row to the root README's adoption table. The landing page never shows a broken badge, and the template keeps the shared shape. The follow-up reaches the maintainer at exactly the release where it becomes possible, and because the steps name no host, they serve any later host too. The release step is then complete enough that the seed also runs promptly, which shortens the distribution repository's broken-strip window. The release skill grows from a pre-flight stop into a post-publish checklist the skill itself does not execute. Its `Release:` commit must still change only version slots and the changelog, so the row lands in a separate hand-made commit. The adoption table is still one repository short at the end of the milestone.

The Codex README template opens with the two `uHappyLogic/cairn-codex` traffic badges, in the same strip shape as the other two host templates. The root README's adoption table gains its `uHappyLogic/cairn-codex` row in the same milestone. Both point at the repository's `traffic-data` branch before that branch exists. No follow-up step is recorded, because each image starts resolving once the first Codex release has been published, `TRAFFIC_TOKEN` has been set on the repository, and the traffic workflow has run once. The milestone ends release-ready in the full sense the goal names. The Codex template matches the other two host templates exactly, the adoption table lists every distribution repository, and nothing about badges is left for anyone to remember after the release. From the milestone's commit until the first Codex release and the seed run, the root README's adoption table shows two broken images under the cairn-codex row, and so does `hosts/codex/README.md` when viewed on `main`. That could last days or weeks. It reverses the milestone 25 precedent of seeding `traffic-data` before any README references the badges. The distribution repository also shows a broken strip from the publish until the first workflow run.

alternative.id: Strip now, row after seed (Out of Scope)

open-question.alternative: The Codex README template carries its badge strip from the start, like the other two host templates, so the first Codex release publishes it. The root README's adoption-table row is not added in this milestone. It is added in a follow-up commit on `main` after the first Codex release has seeded `traffic-data`. The milestone records that follow-up as an entry in its `## Out of Scope` section. The landing page never shows a broken badge, which follows the milestone 25 precedent of seeding before referencing. The template stays identical in shape to the other two, so the distribution repository needs no second release to get its strip. Its strip is broken only from the publish until the first workflow run, which the maintainer controls. The milestone ends with the adoption table one repository short. The follow-up is held only by a note in a milestone that will be finished by then, and nothing prompts the maintainer at the moment the seed run completes, so the row can easily be forgotten. The `hosts/codex/README.md` render on `main` still shows a broken strip until the seed.

Neither reference lands in this milestone. The Codex README template is written without the badge strip, so the first Codex release publishes a README with no traffic badges, and the root adoption table gets no cairn-codex row. Once the first release has seeded `traffic-data`, a follow-up commit adds the strip to the template and the row to the root README, with the Codex tree rebuilt. The strip reaches `uHappyLogic/cairn-codex` at the next release. The milestone records the follow-up in its `## Out of Scope` section. No surface, whether the root README, the `hosts/codex/` render, or the distribution repository, ever shows a broken image. This applies the milestone 25 seed-before-reference rule fully, to the template as well as the root table. The Codex template departs from the shape the other two host templates share. Adding the strip later takes a template edit, a rebuild, and a second release before the distribution repository shows badges. The only thing holding the follow-up is a note in a finished milestone, so the badges can easily stay missing.

Neither reference lands in this milestone. The Codex template is written without the badge strip, and the root adoption table gets no cairn-codex row. The release skill's printed missing-`TRAFFIC_TOKEN` instructions gain steps that name no host. After publishing, run the repository's `traffic-badges` workflow once by `workflow_dispatch`. Then add the repository's badge strip to its host README template and its row to the root README's adoption table, rebuild, and let the next release carry the strip. No surface ever shows a broken image, and the deferred work reaches the maintainer at exactly the release that makes it possible. Because the instructions name no host, every later host reuses them. This has the most moving parts. The template departs from the shared shape until a second release, the release skill gains a post-publish checklist it does not run itself, and the badge additions need their own commit apart from the `Release:` commit. open-question.question: `docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md` will name `codex exec "<prompt>"` as the Codex form of a headless line, whose Claude Code and Antigravity form is `-p "/cairn:<skill>"`. Codex's documented explicit invocation is the `$` sigil, which a shell expands as a variable inside double quotes, and whether Codex accepts `/cairn:<skill>` is unconfirmed. What prompt text, in what quoting, does the page give for invoking a cairn skill through `codex exec`?
open-question.applied-principle: Check tier claims against the live environment
open-question.recommendation: It is Codex's documented explicit invocation with the namespace the README already shows, so users type one form everywhere, and single quotes stop the shell's `$` expansion with no escape character to lose, where a dropped backslash silently sends Codex a truncated prompt and an apostrophe in a goal fails loudly; a `codex debug prompt-input` render on the installed 0.159.3 passes `$` and `/` prompt text through alike and injects no skill for either, so no other form has evidence over the documented one.
open-question.alternative: The page gives `codex exec '$cairn:<skill>'` as the Codex form of a line. The prompt uses Codex's documented `$` sigil with the plugin namespace, which is the same `$cairn:<skill>` text the Codex README already uses. The prompt sits in single quotes so the shell passes the `$` through as written. The swap rule gains one more step: moving a line to Codex also rewrites `"/cairn:<skill>"` to `'$cairn:<skill>'`. The placeholder rule for `<goal>` changes from "no double quote" to "no single quote" on Codex lines. The command uses Codex's documented explicit invocation and the namespace the README already shows, so users type one form in both places. Single quotes are the plain POSIX way to stop `$` expansion and need no escape character that a reader could drop. It breaks the page's double-quote convention. A `<goal>` written in prose often contains an apostrophe, which ends the single-quoted prompt early, so Codex lines need a different placeholder rule from the other hosts. Whether `codex exec` resolves a `$cairn:` mention in its prompt text is still unconfirmed; it holds only if a no-model probe or the live verification checks it, and whether the live run is headless is a separate question.

alternative.id: Namespaced sigil, escaped in double quotes

open-question.alternative: The page gives `codex exec "\$cairn:<skill>"` as the Codex form of a line. The prompt uses the documented `$` sigil with the plugin namespace and stays in double quotes like every other line on the page, with the `$` backslash-escaped so the shell does not expand it. The legend says why the backslash is there. The swap rule adds rewriting `/cairn:` to `\$cairn:` inside the existing quotes. The "no double quote" rule for `<goal>` stays as it is. It keeps the page's one quoting convention and its placeholder rule for every host, so `<goal>` prose with apostrophes still works. It uses the same documented sigil and namespace as the README. The backslash is easy to lose when copying or rewriting a line. If it is lost, the shell silently expands `$cairn` to nothing and Codex receives `:<skill>`, with no error. The escape is POSIX-shell specific. It shares the open point that `$` mentions in `codex exec` prompt text are unconfirmed, which depends on the probes or the live verification.

The page gives `codex exec '$<skill>'`, the unnamespaced `$skillname` form exactly as Codex's skills page writes it, in single quotes so the shell leaves the `$` alone. The swap rule rewrites `"/cairn:<skill>"` to `'$<skill>'`, and Codex lines use the "no single quote" placeholder rule. It is literally the explicit-invocation form Codex documents, so it does not depend on whether Codex accepts a `plugin:` prefix inside a `$` mention. It differs from the namespaced `$cairn:` form the recorded README decision chose, so a user sees two forms. A bare name can collide with a same-named skill from another plugin or from `.agents/skills`. It shares the single-quote apostrophe problem and the unconfirmed resolution of `$` mentions in `codex exec`.

The page gives `codex exec "/cairn:<skill>"`, the same prompt text and double quoting as the Claude Code and Antigravity lines. The swap rule stays as recorded: change the binary invocation, drop `--model` and `--effort`, replace the permission flag, and leave the prompt as it is. There is no `$`, so nothing needs escaping. The prompt text is identical across all three hosts, so the recorded one-line swap rule works as written. It also matches the slash names that the rendered Codex skills use for each other unchanged. Nothing on this machine shows that Codex treats `/cairn:<skill>` as a skill invocation. `codex exec` probably passes it to the model as plain text, so the skill runs only if the model recognises the name. That is a model-judgment path, which the probe decision says the design should not lean on. It also contradicts the `$cairn:` form the README gives.

The page gives a plain-prose prompt that names the skill, such as `codex exec "Run the cairn:<skill> skill"`, in double quotes. It uses no sigil and no slash command and relies on Codex choosing the skill from its name and description. Arguments such as `<goal>` follow the prose. The swap rule rewrites the prompt into that sentence, and the "no double quote" rule stays. It needs no unconfirmed invocation syntax and no shell escaping. Codex documents that skills are picked implicitly from their descriptions, so the line does not depend on how `$` or `/` mentions are parsed in `codex exec`. Which skill runs, and whether one runs at all, is left to the model. Two runs of the same line can differ, which weakens a headless chain where nobody is watching. The prompt wording also becomes a new convention the page has to define and keep stable.

For now the page keeps `codex exec "<prompt>"` with the prompt text unspecified and states no Codex invocation form or quoting. It says only that the prompt invokes the skill. The concrete text and quoting are filled in later in this milestone, once a no-model probe (for example, `codex debug prompt-input` on a prompt with a mention) or the live verification has shown which form Codex resolves. Until then the swap rule covers only the binary and the flags. The page never publishes an invocation form that might not work. The choice rests on the probe evidence the milestone has already committed to gathering, not on guessing between unconfirmed forms. Until the evidence arrives, the page's Codex coverage has no runnable line and the swap rule is incomplete. The open choice comes back as unfinished documentation work. Whether it can close inside the milestone depends on a probe giving a clear answer or on the live run being headless, and the run mode is a separate question.

open-question.question: The build script gains a new operation (named wording slots in `core/` filled from a new per-host settings key), and no test under `tests/` covers `scripts/build_hosts.py` today; the only checks are the build's own validation gate, `--check`, and the byte-identity diff of the two existing host trees. Does this milestone add automated tests for the new slot operation, and if so, covering what?
open-question.recommendation: The byte-identity bar already tests the substitution end to end, since every slot site must reproduce the released Claude Code and Antigravity bytes through the same code path that renders Codex, and an unfilled slot already fails the build; the one hole left is a host declaring a slot core/ never uses or a slot set that differs between hosts, which this check closes in the gate where every other build invariant lives, with no fixture skeleton and no skipped file at the 3.9 floor.
open-question.alternative: No pytest tests are added. `scripts/build_hosts.py` instead gets one more named check in its validation gate, run on every build and on every CI `--check`. The check fails when any host declares a slot name that appears nowhere in `core/`, or when the set of declared slot names differs between hosts. A slot used in `core/` but missing from a host is still left to the existing `unfilled-placeholder` check. The check is added to the script's docstring list of checks. The rule "every host declares every slot", which the wording-mechanism decision states but nothing enforces in full, is enforced at the point where a definition is edited. Because it lives in the same gate as every other build invariant, it needs no new test infrastructure, no `tomllib`/`yaml` handling at the 3.9 floor, and no change to the CI job. A check confirms that the definitions are consistent. It does not confirm that the substitution itself is correct, so a bug in how slot values are written into the text (wrong order next to `{{PLUGIN_ROOT}}`, a value applied to templates, or left out of them, when it should not be) is still caught only by diffs. The check itself is also untested code.

The milestone adds no automated test for the slot operation and leaves `tests/` and `scripts/build_hosts.py`'s check set as they are. The new operation is guarded only by what exists today plus what the wording-mechanism decision already names: the settings schema's missing-or-unknown-key build error, which covers the new settings key once it joins the schema, and the `unfilled-placeholder` check, which catches a slot a host fails to fill. Behind those sit `--check` in the drift-gate CI job, the byte-identity diff of `hosts/claude/` and `hosts/antigravity/` against `5305f43`, and the live Codex verification run. Any test suite for the build script is left to a later milestone of its own, if one is ever wanted. It costs nothing, and the preservation bar already gives the strongest regression evidence available. A slot operation that broke the Claude Code or Antigravity output would show up as a non-empty byte diff against `5305f43` and as `--check` drift. A slot left unfilled anywhere already fails the build. The Codex side of the operation is checked only by eye. Nothing automated checks that a Codex slot value reaches the right place, that a slot sitting next to `{{PLUGIN_ROOT}}` or a `${{ … }}` expression renders correctly, or that a host declaring a slot `core/` never uses is noticed. The build script stays the one shipped piece of code without a test, and the first future change to the slot code has nothing to catch a regression.

A new test file under `tests/` covers only the slot operation and the existing gates it relies on, and the build gets no new check. It runs the build against a minimal fixture `core/` and fixture host definitions set up in a temporary repository skeleton: a copy of the script beside its own `core/`, `scripts/hosts/`, `VERSION`, `LICENSE` and root marketplace, since every input path is derived from the script's own location. The tests check that: - each slot is filled with each host's value; - text with no slot comes out byte-identical; - a slot sitting next to `{{PLUGIN_ROOT}}` and a `${{ … }}` expression renders correctly; - a host missing a slot value fails `unfilled-placeholder` with exit 1; - a missing or wrongly typed slot settings key fails as an unusable definition with exit 2. Whether the tests run the script as a subprocess or call it in-process with the path constants patched is left to the task. The file skips itself at module level when `tomllib` or `yaml` cannot be imported, so the `--no-project` 3.9 floor run still passes. The `tests/` line in `CLAUDE.md`, which today scopes the suite to `core/tools/`, is widened to include the build. The one new piece of build behaviour, and the only one whose Codex output has no committed baseline to diff against, gets checks that state what it should do. The added code stays small, uses the suite's existing end-to-end style, and leaves the unchanged parts of the build to `--check` and the preservation bar. It adds the suite's first test of code outside `core/tools/`, needs a new fixture skeleton, and makes the 3.9 floor run report a skip rather than covering the file. The rest of `scripts/build_hosts.py` (renames, exclude, frontmatter stripping, every other check) stays untested. A declared-but-unused slot also still goes unnoticed, because no check exists for the tests to exercise.

This combines the two options above. The build gains the declared-slot consistency check from "Build-gate check only": it fails when a host declares a slot `core/` never uses, or when the hosts' slot-name sets differ. The focused slot test file from "Focused slot tests" is added under `tests/`, with the same fixture skeleton, module-level skip at the 3.9 floor, and widened `CLAUDE.md` `tests/` line. It also has cases that trigger the new check from both directions and assert its named failure and exit 1. Both halves of the operation are covered. The gate enforces that the definitions stay consistent on every build, and the tests pin down both the substitution and the gate's own behaviour. Each new line of build code in this milestone ships with a test that would catch it breaking. It is the largest slot-only change: a new check, a new fixture skeleton, and a test file, all for an operation whose Claude Code and Antigravity output is already locked by the byte-identity bar. The rest of the build script stays untested.

The milestone adds a test suite for the whole of `scripts/build_hosts.py`, and the slot operation is one part of it. The build gets no new check beyond what the wording-mechanism decision names. The suite uses the fixture-skeleton approach and the module-level skip at the 3.9 floor described in "Focused slot tests", and the `CLAUDE.md` `tests/` line is widened. It covers: - **Text operations:** the slot cases; `{{PLUGIN_ROOT}}` replacement; prose-drop patterns; frontmatter-key stripping; renames and exclude, including the both-render-to-one-path error. - **Templates:** rendering of `{{VERSION}}` and `{{NAME}}`. - **Gate checks:** each named check, with a failing and a passing case. - **Settings and drift:** settings-schema errors, and the `--check` comparison with its exit statuses 0, 1 and 2. It closes a long-standing gap at the moment the build becomes more complex. The milestone changes the script for a third host, and Codex is the first host whose tree has no released baseline. With the suite in place, a later change to any operation or check is caught by a test instead of by noticing a diff. Most of the work tests code this milestone does not touch, which widens the scope well beyond what Codex support needs. Even "release-ready" Codex support does not require it, and a suite this size has to be kept up to date as the build changes in later milestones.

open-question.question: The live Codex verification (plugin install, one inline skill, one dispatch of each agent) can be run headless through `codex exec` with the approval-and-sandbox bypass, or as an interactive session under the workspace-write sandbox that the Codex instructions describe to users, where every git staging and commit step asks for approval. In which mode is the live verification run, and is it carried out by the task runner or by the maintainer by hand?
open-question.recommendation: Each documented configuration gets a live check inside the same four runs: the one interactive check carries the fewest approval prompts yet backs the README's invocation form and both sandbox claims in the default configuration the Codex instructions describe, and the approval-heavy dispatches run unattended in the headless form the docs page documents; headless-only would leave every interactive claim unverified and interactive-only every headless one, and the single handover to the maintainer falls at the milestone's last task.
open-question.alternative: The checks are split by mode, and each still runs exactly once. The task runner does the no-model plugin install. It then runs the dispatch of each agent as a headless `codex exec` run with `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` in the temporary workspace, calling Codex by its full path. The maintainer runs the one inline skill by hand in an interactive session under the documented workspace-write sandbox with on-request approval, invoking it as `$cairn:<skill>` and approving its git steps. The runner records all four outcomes in `TASKS_DONE.md`. Both documented configurations get one live check each, with no extra free-tier quota spent. The interactive check is the one with the fewest approval prompts, so the sandbox and approval claims are confirmed cheaply. The approval-heavy agent dispatches run unattended in the headless form. The verification needs both the maintainer and the runner, and they have to hand over between them, so neither the runner alone nor the maintainer alone can finish it. Each configuration is shown working for only part of the surface: agent dispatch is never seen under the sandbox, and an inline skill is never seen headless. The headless half still depends on the prompt text that the sibling question on the headless prompt form decides, and the runner may be refused permission to start Codex with the bypass flag.

alternative.id: Headless, run by the task runner

open-question.alternative: The task runner runs every live check itself, in the verification workspace, as part of the verification task. The plugin install is the no-model `codex plugin marketplace add` and `codex plugin add` step. The inline skill and the dispatch of each agent are separate non-interactive `codex exec` runs carrying `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` and `-C` pointed at the temporary repository. The runner calls Codex by its full path, because `~/.local/bin` is not on a non-login shell's PATH. The runner reads each run's output and the repository's resulting commits and files, then writes the result into `TASKS_DONE.md` through the completion procedure. The maintainer has no part in the run. It needs no human at the keyboard. It runs exactly the headless form the Codex docs and `docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md` will document. Its evidence is the repository state the runs leave behind, checked the same way for every check. Under the quota-exhaustion fallback, the task simply stops on a resumable tree and picks up at the first unrun check. It never runs the interactive workspace-write configuration that the Codex instructions tell users to use. So the claims that each git staging and commit step asks for approval, and that the `python3` tools need only read access to the plugin directory, stay unverified. It also has an agent start a second agent with every sandbox and approval check turned off, which the runner's own permission settings may refuse. Whether each run invokes the right skill depends on the prompt text for invoking a skill through `codex exec`, which the sibling question on the headless prompt form decides.

alternative.id: Headless, run by the maintainer by hand

open-question.alternative: The maintainer runs the same commands from a login shell: the no-model install step, then one `codex exec` run with `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` for the inline skill and for each agent dispatch, all in the temporary workspace. The maintainer then gives the outcomes to the verification task. The runner only records those outcomes in `TASKS_DONE.md` and starts no Codex run itself. A person decides when each run spends scarce free-tier quota and judges each result as it lands. No agent ever starts a second agent with sandboxing turned off. The headless form the docs will document still gets exercised. The task runner cannot finish the verification task alone. It has to stop and wait for the maintainer, which breaks a headless `complete-all-tasks` chain. The interactive sandboxed configuration given to users still goes unverified. And whether each run invokes the right skill still depends on the prompt text that the sibling question on the headless prompt form decides.

alternative.id: Interactive sandboxed, run by the maintainer

open-question.alternative: The maintainer runs every model check in one or more interactive Codex sessions. These use the configuration the Codex instructions give users: the workspace-write sandbox with the on-request approval policy, and no change to `config.toml`. The maintainer invokes the skills the way the README documents (`$cairn:<skill>`) and approves each git staging and commit request as it comes. The plugin install is the same no-model CLI step. No `codex exec` run and no bypass flag is used, and the runner only records the outcomes in `TASKS_DONE.md`. It checks exactly what a Codex user will meet: the README's invocation form, the claim that each git step asks for approval, and the claim that the plugin's `python3` tools run with read-only access to the installed plugin directory. Every word the user-facing instructions say about the sandbox is then backed by a live run. It needs a person for the whole run, and the agent dispatches need many approvals: `complete-all-tasks` and the alternatives pass each stage and commit. The task runner cannot carry out the verification task. The documented `codex exec` headless form is never run live, so the headless claims in `docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md` rest on `--help` output alone.

open-question.question: Several recorded decisions rest on Codex behaviour that is still unverified (that `${PLUGIN_ROOT}` reaches the commands a skill runs, that a generic subagent can be spawned and told to read a plugin file, that the marketplace layout installs), and the no-model probes and the live run that would confirm them happen after those decisions were recorded. When a probe or the live verification contradicts a recorded decision, how does the milestone proceed?

recommendation.option: Probe before task derivation, reopen on contradiction

open-question.recommendation: It restores the probe decision's intent of settling behaviours before the work that depends on them: the no-model probes run while the milestone is still in the question loop, so most contradictions are corrected by the documented revert-then-re-answer before any task is written against a false premise, and a contradiction only the live run can find is reopened the same way with its fix submitted as new tasks; the inline-adapting option lets a completion runner make a requirements decision, the pre-recorded fallbacks contradict the plugin-root decision's stated no-fallback, and halting or narrowing pays its cost after implementation.

alternative.id: Probe before task derivation, reopen on contradiction

open-question.alternative: The no-model probes run as a requirements-phase step outside the task list, before derive-tasks runs. Any contradiction they find goes into the starting state and is corrected by revert-then-re-answer while the milestone is still in the question loop and no Codex implementation exists. Only the live verification can then contradict a decision after implementation. In that case the decision is reopened the same way, and the fix goes in as new tasks through submit-task while the milestone stays open. Most of the unverified premises (that ${PLUGIN_ROOT} reaches skill commands, that the marketplace layout installs, how installed agents are presented) get checked before any task is written against them. That matches the probe decision's intent to settle behaviours before the decisions that depend on them, and contradictions surface while they are still cheap. The milestone gains a manual pre-derivation step that falls outside the normal pipeline. The maintainer has to run the probes and fold the findings in by hand before derive-tasks can start. The runtime-only behaviours that only the live run can settle still carry the late-rework risk.

alternative.id: Halt and reopen through the answer workflow

open-question.alternative: The process is the same whether the contradiction comes from a no-model probe or from the live verification. The task that finds it stops and returns FAILED, leaving the tree resumable, and the whole task list halts behind it. The finding goes into the relevant starting state. The maintainer corrects the contradicted decision the way the project already corrects a bad answer: revert its answer commit so the question reopens, then run the alternatives, recommendation and answer passes again. The tasks the new decision affects are then rewritten or derived again, and only after that does task completion resume. Work already done on the old decision is kept or reworked by those revised tasks and is never reverted wholesale. Every changed decision goes through the same recorded route as the first one. That means an answer commit capture can read, a human choice of the replacement, and no work built further on a premise known to be false. It also needs no new mechanism, because revert-then-re-answer is already the documented way to correct an answer. Any contradiction freezes the whole milestone, including tasks it does not touch, until a full question cycle has run again. If the contradiction appears only at the live verification, the rework comes after implementation and costs another session of free-tier quota.

The finding goes into the starting state. The contradicted decision is reopened, either by revert-then-re-answer or by a superseding question that the next review pass raises, and it is answered through the normal answer workflow. Only tasks that depend on the contradicted decision wait. Every task that does not rest on it keeps running in the meantime. After the new answer is recorded, the dependent tasks are revised and completed. A narrow contradiction, such as one about marketplace layout, stops only the work it actually affects. The rest of the Codex host (the wording slots, the docs, the release-skill check) keeps moving, and each changed decision still gets a human answer with provenance. Someone has to judge which tasks depend on which unverified behaviour, and nothing recorded encodes that. An open question would also stand while tasks are being completed, which the derive-tasks precondition was meant to exclude. Finally, work done in the meantime may itself be shaped by the decision that later changes.

Any decision is reopened only if the contradicted decision has no working replacement. Otherwise the task that finds the contradiction chooses the nearest working replacement itself, for example another plugin-root form, another dispatch form or another install layout. In the same task it rewrites the affected Decisions entry and the starting state, implements the replacement, and continues. The change is visible only in that task's commit and its Verified record. No extra session, no stop, and no new question cycle. That counts for a lot when live runs are scarce on a free-tier account and the replacement is often the obvious next form. A dispatched or inline completion runner makes a requirements decision without a human. That bypasses the answer workflow, so no answer commit exists for capture to learn from, and it breaks the separation between recording decisions and completing tasks. How much the runner can adapt during the live run depends on the axis the "Verification run mode" sibling owns: who runs the verification, the task runner or the maintainer.

Before any probe runs, every decision that rests on unverified Codex behaviour gets a named fallback in Decisions. The decisions covered are the plugin-root literal, the generic-subagent agent form, and the subdirectory marketplace layout. For example, a different root literal or a prose plugin-root path, running the agent procedure inline when a generic subagent cannot follow a plugin file, and another install layout. When a probe or the live run contradicts the primary choice, the task switches to the recorded fallback with no reopen. Only a contradiction with no recorded fallback, or a failed fallback, stops the milestone for a reopen. A human chooses the response to each foreseeable contradiction now, while the context is fresh. A contradiction found mid-milestone then becomes an applied decision rather than a stop, and the quota-limited live run does not wait on a new question cycle. It adds design work for outcomes that may never happen. The fallbacks are themselves unverified, so they can be contradicted too. It also conflicts with the plugin-root decision's explicit "There is no fallback", which would itself have to be reopened.

alternative.id: Narrow scope to what is verified

open-question.alternative: A contradicted capability is not redesigned. It is declared unsupported on Codex instead. Examples: the agents run inline rather than as subagents on Codex, or the install route the probes could not confirm is dropped. modify-milestone-goal records this as a goal change, together with an Out of Scope entry and matching wording in the Codex README. The milestone finishes on the capabilities that were confirmed, and the contradicted capability is left to a later milestone. A contradiction can never send the milestone through rounds of redesign and repeated live runs on a free-tier quota. Every claim the release makes is still backed by the verification that actually passed. The milestone may ship short of its goal of running the whole pipeline, including both dispatched agents, on Codex. It gives up a redesign that might have been cheap, and it makes Codex a lesser host from its first release.

The milestone records no procedure for contradictions. If one arises, the maintainer handles it case by case when it happens, using the project's existing conventions: revert-then-re-answer, review passes, submit-task, and modify-milestone-goal. No up-front rule for a situation that may never come up. Each response can be fitted to what was actually contradicted, using conventions the project already documents. The task runner has no instruction at the moment it meets a contradiction, so it may adapt silently, fail without guidance, or work on top of a false premise. Which response to choose is then decided under time and quota pressure mid-milestone instead of now.
